question: Does ReLU spectral bias arise from ill-conditioning of its finite-element basis, and can replacing ReLU with a compact piecewise-linear Hat activation equalize frequency learning and accelerate neural function fitting?

key_findings.claim: The intended theoretical mechanism is basis conditioning: for a one-dimensional shallow network with fixed equally spaced inner units and trainable output coefficients, gradient descent follows the eigenvalues of an activation Gram matrix.
key_findings.evidence: The paper maps translated ReLU and scaled Hat units to two bases of a linear finite-element space. It claims the ReLU mass-matrix spectrum has condition ratios proportional to n^4/j^4, while the Hat mass matrix has bounded condition number, so low-roughness ReLU modes contract much faster and Hat modes contract at comparable rates. This is a finite-width linear least-squares analysis, not an NTK limit.

anchors.section: Theorems 1-3, mass-matrix spectrum and gradient descent
Appendix A.2, ReLU and Hat finite-element bases

key_findings.claim: Within the corrected finite-element setup, ReLU and Hat units span the same function space, so the result demonstrates an optimizer-coordinate or preconditioning effect rather than a difference in representational capacity.
key_findings.evidence: Appendix A.2 explicitly gives an invertible second-difference matrix C with Phi=C Psi, converting the global ReLU ramp basis into local Hat functions. The two parameterizations therefore express identical piecewise-linear functions. Euclidean gradient descent is not invariant to this non-orthogonal change of coordinates: the ReLU coefficient Gram matrix is ill-conditioned and the localized Hat basis is well-conditioned. A basis-invariant optimizer or an appropriate preconditioner could remove the difference without changing the activation family.

key_findings.claim: The displayed shallow network is not the finite-element system analyzed in the appendix: it contains an identically zero final unit, contradicting the claimed positive definiteness.
key_findings.evidence: Equation 7 sums ReLU(x-i/n) for i=1 through n on [0,1]. The i=n function is ReLU(x-1), which is zero everywhere on that interval up to a measure-zero endpoint, so its Gram matrix has a zero row and column and cannot be positive definite. Appendix A.2 silently uses knots x_(i-1), including zero and ending at (n-1)/n, and also scales the ramps by 1/h. That shifted basis can be nonsingular, but it is not Equation 7; the main theorems therefore do not apply as written.

key_findings.claim: The quadratic-loss and gradient-descent statement contains three additional mathematical errors, although its intended finite-dimensional contraction formula is recognizable.
key_findings.evidence: For L=(1/2) integral (u-f)^2 with M defined by basis inner products, Equation 9 should contain (1/2)a^TMa, an additive constant, and -b^Ta; it instead prints a^TMa-b^Ta. With the printed objective, step 1/lambda_max gives a largest-mode factor of -1 rather than the stated contraction. Equation 16 is self-referential, alpha_i^ell=alpha_i^ell(1-lambda_i/lambda_n)^ell, where the right initial coefficient should be alpha_i^0. Finally, Equation 15 expands arbitrary u-f in the n-dimensional model span without assuming u belongs to it; Section 3 correctly used f_ell-f_star instead.

anchors.section: Equations 9 and 14-16, quadratic form and mode dynamics

key_findings.claim: The main theorem equating frequency with an L2 norm of a second derivative is undefined for the piecewise-linear functions under study and is not proved by the appendix's discrete-difference calculation.
key_findings.evidence: Theorem 4 prints the integral of |phi_j double-prime| squared divided by the L2 norm. A nontrivial continuous piecewise-linear finite-element function has a weak second derivative consisting of Dirac masses, not an L2 function, so this numerator is not finite or defined. Appendix Theorem 7 instead proves a ratio for D_h, explicitly a second-order finite-difference operator on nodal values. A discrete roughness statement may support the plots, but it does not imply the classical derivative equation printed in Theorem 4.

anchors.section: Appendix A.5, Theorem 7 and discrete D_h
Equation 68 and claimed implication to Theorem 4

key_findings.claim: The empirical suite consistently shows faster target-frequency fitting with Hat activations across low-dimensional signals, deep coordinate networks, image regression, SGD, Adam, and an MNIST kernel-eigenfunction diagnostic.
key_findings.evidence: Fourier-mode errors for one- and two-dimensional sinusoidal targets separate in order for tanh/ReLU but converge together for Hat. In the six-layer example, the reported ReLU loss remains about 10^-3 after 80,000 epochs while a Hat network reaches about 10^-22 after 800; a grayscale image retains more detail under Hat. Appendix experiments repeat the qualitative ordering in two and three dimensions, with fewer neurons, SGD, wider ReLU models, a phase-shift baseline, and a sine activation. On 2,000 noisy MNIST images, Hat kernel modes reportedly converge by iteration 200 while high-frequency ReLU modes lag.

anchors.section: Experiments 3-4, deep fitting speed and image regression

key_findings.claim: The headline training-speed comparisons are not controlled activation ablations because initialization scale, learning rate, decay schedule, width, and sometimes architecture change together, with no repeated-run uncertainty.
key_findings.evidence: Experiment 1 initializes ReLU/tanh at standard deviation 0.1 and Hat at 0.8. Experiment 2 gives Hat a learning rate fifteen times ReLU's. Experiment 3 changes Gaussian versus broad uniform initialization, learning rate by factors up to 100, decay cadence, and one Hat width; Experiment 4 uses different decay intervals. The phase-shift comparison pits sixteen deep ReLU models against one very wide shallow Hat model. Some appendix experiments do match learning rates and initial ranges, but the paper supplies no systematic hyperparameter sweep, seed count, error bars, hardware, wall time, or per-step cost.

anchors.section: Experiments 1-2, unmatched initialization and learning rates

key_findings.claim: Removing low-frequency preference is not uniformly a generalization advantage: it also accelerates fitting high-frequency noise, and the paper does not itself demonstrate improved classification generalization.
key_findings.evidence: Experiments 5-7 deliberately add high-frequency noise to a smooth target. ReLU first reaches the clean low-frequency function and only later fits the noise, producing an early-stopping dip; Hat learns the noise without this delay. That is useful when high frequencies are signal but removes a regularizing window when they are noise. The MNIST study fits 2,000 noisy training labels and reports spectral convergence only—no held-out accuracy, calibration, robustness, or comparison on clean classification. The abstract's image-classification benefit is attributed to a separate prior paper.

key_findings.claim: The theory is much narrower than the paper's deep-network conclusions, and its frequency axes change across sections in ways that preclude one universal activation law.
key_findings.evidence: The proof trains output coefficients only, at fixed one-dimensional knots, with exact population L2 loss and full-batch gradient descent. Deep experiments train every weight with Adam or SGD under task-specific Hat scales such as 100 and 200. The theory's modes are eigenvectors of an activation-dependent mass matrix; synthetic experiments use Fourier modes; MNIST uses eigenvectors of an RBF kernel whose bandwidth and digit pair are not reported. These can all be useful diagnostics, but no theorem connects the fixed-basis condition number to trainable deep Hat networks or to arbitrary data-kernel frequencies.

method.core_idea: Interpret translated ReLU ramps and compact Hat functions as alternative bases for the same piecewise-linear finite-element space, relate their Gram-matrix condition numbers to gradient-descent mode speeds, and test whether localized Hat activations flatten the empirical frequency-learning profile.
method.mechanism: The theory fixes one-dimensional inner weights and knots and trains only output coefficients under integrated squared loss. Eigenanalysis of the basis mass matrix is meant to show an n^4 ReLU conditioning gap versus bounded Hat conditioning, with a discrete roughness calculation linking slow modes to oscillation. Experiments then train shallow and deep networks with unscaled or input-scaled Hat activations on sinusoidal regression, clean targets plus high-frequency noise, grayscale image fitting, and noisy two-class MNIST; Fourier coefficients or Gaussian-RBF kernel eigenvectors serve as frequency coordinates.
assumptions: The main-text fixed ReLU basis matches the nonsingular shifted basis in the appendix despite their one-index difference.
The printed quadratic form and mode-recursion equations can be silently corrected without changing the conclusions.
A discrete second-difference roughness result may be interpreted as an L2 norm of the classical second derivative of a piecewise-linear function.
Conditioning of an output-only fixed-feature regression predicts all-parameter optimization in deep networks.
Activation-dependent mass eigenmodes, Fourier modes, and data-kernel eigenvectors capture a sufficiently common notion of frequency.
Task-specific Hat scales keep enough units in their compact support to avoid dead gradients and yield a fair comparison with ReLU.
Method-specific initialization and optimizer schedules are close to each method's optimum and do not create the observed speed ordering.
Single-run curve comparisons represent typical behavior over phases, samples, and initialization seeds.
Learning all high frequencies rapidly is desirable even when high-frequency components are label or measurement noise.

techniques.role: Maps translated ReLU ramps and compact Hat units to global and local bases of one spline space.
Uses basis Gram eigenvalues to predict unequal or equal gradient-descent mode contraction.
Replaces ReLU with a triangular piecewise-linear function supported on a bounded preactivation interval.
Adjusts support and nominal frequency through Hat(alpha times p) for each task.
Tracks normalized target-frequency coefficient errors throughout regression training.
Varies the frequency of additive training noise while validating against the clean low-frequency function.
Orders sparse high-dimensional MNIST label components using Gaussian-RBF kernel eigenvectors.
Checks the qualitative effect across Adam, SGD, smaller Hat networks, and increasing ReLU width.

limitations: Author-stated: the analysis covers only the ReLU/Hat fixed-feature construction and a broader activation-function theory remains future work.
Reviewer-identified: Equation 7 has an identically zero final ReLU feature, so its mass matrix is singular rather than positive definite.
Reviewer-identified: the appendix uses a shifted and scaled basis different from Equation 7 without reconciling the definitions.
Reviewer-identified: Equation 9 drops the one-half quadratic coefficient and additive constant required by Equation 8.
Reviewer-identified: Equation 16 is self-referential and must use an initial coefficient on its right-hand side.
Reviewer-identified: the expansion of u-f in Equation 15 is invalid for arbitrary targets outside the finite model span.
Reviewer-identified: Theorem 4 takes an L2 norm of the second derivative of a piecewise-linear function; the appendix proves only a discrete finite-difference quantity.
Reviewer-identified: the proof is output-only, one-dimensional, fixed-grid, exact-loss gradient descent and does not analyze trained hidden weights, depth, minibatching, Adam, or classification.
Reviewer-identified: ReLU and Hat bases span the same finite-element space, so the theorem is primarily about parameterization-dependent conditioning.
Reviewer-identified: central speed comparisons change initialization, learning rate, decay schedule, width, or architecture in addition to activation.
Reviewer-identified: no seed counts, uncertainty bands, hyperparameter-sweep protocol, wall-clock timings, hardware, or code provenance are reported.
Reviewer-identified: the compact Hat's scale is task tuned, but sensitivity to support width, input normalization, and dead-unit rates is not measured.
Reviewer-identified: the MNIST protocol omits digit identities, RBF bandwidth, architecture, optimizer details, and held-out classification accuracy.
Reviewer-identified: the paper's image-classification generalization statement comes from prior work rather than an experiment in this paper.
Reviewer-identified: removing spectral bias also removes delayed fitting of high-frequency noise, so faster convergence is not synonymous with better generalization.
Reviewer-identified: the phase-shift comparison is not architecture-, depth-, or schedule-matched.
failure_modes: A compact activation can leave most units outside support, producing zero gradients when input scale or initialization is mismatched.
A task-specific Hat scale can leak target-frequency knowledge and fail when the spectrum changes spatially or over time.
Rapid high-frequency learning can memorize label noise, aliasing, or measurement artifacts before early stopping can isolate smooth signal.
Comparing epochs under different schedules and architectures can make conditioning improvements look like activation-only speedups.
Kernel-eigenvector frequency depends on kernel family and bandwidth; an arbitrary choice can reorder what is called low or high frequency.
Localized units can require exponentially many centers in higher dimensions or sparse coverage of the input domain.
A basis-conditioned result can disappear under natural-gradient, second-order, adaptive, or explicitly preconditioned optimization.
High-frequency accuracy at selected target modes can coexist with large off-target spectral artifacts that the reported metric does not show.
Deep compositions of compact Hat units can fragment support and block gradient propagation even when a shallow layer is well conditioned.
An uncorrected index shift or loss normalization can invalidate numerical reproductions of the theorem despite apparently similar plots.
reusable_insights: Separate function-space expressivity from coefficient-space conditioning: compare bases of the same span under explicit preconditioners.
Use localized spline or wavelet bases when uniform spatial coverage and multi-frequency fitting are desired, but expose the support scale as a validated hyperparameter.
Benchmark activation changes with identical initialization statistics, optimizer searches, schedules, parameter counts, per-step compute, and repeated seeds.
Report on-target and off-target spectra, clean-signal validation, and noise memorization to distinguish faster fitting from useful inductive bias.
State frequency operators completely, including kernel, bandwidth, normalization, eigengaps, and stability across choices.
For targets outside a finite feature span, decompose error into learnable projection and irreducible orthogonal residual before deriving mode dynamics.
Write discrete roughness theorems with D_h explicitly rather than substituting classical derivatives unavailable for splines.
Test whether basis reparameterization, Fourier features, or gradient preconditioning reproduces an activation's benefit without compact-support failure modes.
Measure active-unit fraction and gradient connectivity layer by layer for compact activations.
Treat spectral bias as tunable: low-frequency preference can regularize noisy tasks, while balanced or high-frequency learning helps exact signal representation.
open_questions: After correcting the knot indexing, loss normalization, residual projection, and discrete derivative, which parts of the finite-element theorem remain unchanged?
Can an explicit preconditioner for the ReLU coefficient basis exactly reproduce Hat dynamics while preserving ReLU implementation advantages?
How does Hat support scale interact with input dimension, data density, depth, normalization, and trainable hidden features?
Is there a principled way to adapt frequency bias over training so early low-frequency regularization precedes later detail recovery?
Do Hat networks improve held-out accuracy, robustness, and calibration on modern vision, audio, PDE, and neural-field tasks under matched compute?
How stable are MNIST data-kernel frequency conclusions across RBF bandwidths, kernels, class pairs, and eigenspace degeneracies?
Can wavelet or spline activations provide localized multi-resolution coverage without dead gradients in high dimensions?
What optimizer-invariant definition can separate architectural spectral bias from coordinate-dependent gradient conditioning?
Does rapid convergence of selected target Fourier coefficients introduce off-target harmonics or spatial ringing?
Can a common benchmark compare Hat, SIREN, Fourier features, BACON, WIRE, FINER, ReLU wavelets, and reparameterized ReLU across signal and noise regimes?

competitive_landscape.title: On the Spectral Bias of Neural Networks
competitive_landscape.relationship: foundational spectral-bias formulation and primary baseline
competitive_landscape.difference: Rahaman et al. establish low-frequency preference and relate ReLU expressivity to data-manifold complexity and parameter sensitivity. The reviewed paper attempts a finite-element conditioning explanation and a compact-activation intervention, but its experiments closely reuse this earlier setup and its proof is far narrower than the original network-level phenomenon.

competitive_landscape.title: A Fine-Grained Spectral Perspective on Neural Networks
competitive_landscape.relationship: alternative kernel-spectrum theory of activation and optimization bias
competitive_landscape.difference: Yang and Salman analyze conjugate-kernel and NTK spectra across activations, depth, training regimes, and high-dimensional distributions, and show initialization can change spectral behavior. Their framework treats the whole random-network kernel; the reviewed paper instead studies an exact finite-width but output-only deterministic basis Gram matrix.

competitive_landscape.title: Fourier Features Let Networks Learn High Frequency Functions in Low Dimensional Domains
competitive_landscape.relationship: established input-encoding remedy for spectral bias
competitive_landscape.difference: Fourier features retain a standard MLP and tune the effective NTK bandwidth through a sinusoidal input map, with image and 3D graphics evaluations. This separates frequency access from the nonlinear activation and offers a direct alternative to task-scaled compact Hat units.

competitive_landscape.title: Implicit Neural Representations with Periodic Activation Functions
competitive_landscape.difference: SIREN couples sine activations to a principled initialization and demonstrates images, audio, video, derivatives, wavefields, and PDE boundary-value problems. The reviewed paper observes sine spectral ordering in one toy experiment but does not engage SIREN's initialization or broad derivative-based validation.

competitive_landscape.title: BACON: Band-limited Coordinate Networks for Multiscale Scene Representation
competitive_landscape.difference: BACON builds an analytically controllable Fourier spectrum and produces outputs at multiple scales for images, radiance fields, and signed-distance scenes. Rather than eliminating frequency preference, it constrains and exposes bandwidth, which is safer for anti-aliasing and noisy or unsupervised points than uniformly fast high-frequency fitting.

competitive_landscape.title: Spectral Bias in Practice: The Role of Function Frequency in Generalization
competitive_landscape.difference: Fridovich-Keil et al. measure learned-function frequency on CIFAR-10 and ImageNet across architectures, augmentation, data size, and distillation, finding that useful frequency behavior is local and tied to generalization. This supplies the modern held-out classification evidence absent from the reviewed paper's noisy MNIST fitting diagnostic.

competitive_landscape.title: WIRE: Wavelet Implicit Neural Representations
competitive_landscape.relationship: later localized activation with explicit space-frequency design
competitive_landscape.difference: WIRE uses complex Gabor wavelet activations that are localized in both space and frequency, and evaluates denoising, inpainting, super-resolution, CT, image fitting, and NeRF. It targets the Hat activation's localization intuition while directly testing robustness to noise and parameter variation.

competitive_landscape.title: Understanding the Spectral Bias of Coordinate Based MLPs Via Training Dynamics
competitive_landscape.difference: Lazzari and Liu analyze ReLU activation regions and spatial training dynamics rather than an output-only fixed basis, and explain how positional encoding changes those dynamics. This more directly targets the trainable coordinate-MLP regime used in the reviewed deep experiments.

competitive_landscape.title: FINER: Flexible Spectral-bias Tuning in Implicit Neural Representation by Variable-periodic Activation Functions
competitive_landscape.difference: FINER uses a variable-periodic activation whose supported frequency set is adjusted through bias initialization and validates images, signed-distance fields, and radiance fields. It treats spectral bias as tunable rather than simply removable and studies a broader INR task suite.

competitive_landscape.title: Improved Implicit Neural Representation with Fourier Reparameterized Training
competitive_landscape.difference: Fourier reparameterized training explicitly argues that optimization coordinates reshape spectral bias and composes weights from fixed Fourier bases across vanilla, encoded, and advanced-activation MLPs. It reinforces the reviewer interpretation that the reviewed finite-element result is fundamentally a parameterization/preconditioning result, not solely an activation-capacity result.

competitive_landscape.title: ReLUs Are Sufficient for Learning Implicit Neural Representations
competitive_landscape.difference: Shenouda et al. impose simple second-order B-spline-wavelet-inspired constraints on ReLU neurons and report state-of-the-art signal representation, super-resolution, and CT results. This shows compact localized basis behavior can be engineered from ReLUs, weakening any practical need to replace the activation outright.

novelty_assessment.author_claim: The paper claims a finite-width finite-element explanation of ReLU spectral bias, predicts that a compact piecewise-linear Hat activation removes it, and reports dramatically faster Adam and SGD training across synthetic, image, and MNIST settings.
novelty_assessment.evidence: The central constructive insight is an explicit conversion between global ReLU ramps and local Hat bases of a one-dimensional spline space, whose mass matrices have very different conditioning. A broad collection of frequency-trajectory plots consistently favors Hat on exact high-frequency fitting, including deep networks and a data-kernel MNIST diagnostic.
novelty_assessment.reviewer_inference: The localized-basis insight is valuable and anticipates later wavelet, reparameterization, and constrained-ReLU work. Its most defensible theoretical lesson is that gradient spectral bias can be strongly changed by coordinates or preconditioning even when the represented function space is identical. However, the published theorem chain has several non-cosmetic defects: Equation 7 makes the mass matrix singular, the appendix analyzes a shifted basis, the loss normalization and recursion are wrong, arbitrary residuals are expanded in a finite span, and a discrete second difference is presented as an L2 classical second derivative that does not exist. The deep empirical claim remains suggestive but uses unmatched initialization and optimization with no repeats, while faster high-frequency fitting also accelerates noise memorization and no held-out classification benefit is shown. Modern Fourier features, SIREN, BACON, WIRE, FINER, Fourier reparameterization, and ReLU-wavelet constraints offer better-controlled and broader alternatives. Treat this as a provocative basis-conditioning hypothesis with strong toy evidence, not a validated general activation law.

reviewer_notes: Read all 24 extracted pages end to end, including every experiment and the complete finite-element appendix. Rendered PDF pages 5 and 6 were visually inspected at original resolution to verify that Equation 9 really omits the one-half factor, Equation 16 is self-referential, and Theorem 4 really prints a classical double prime rather than the appendix's D_h. Equation 7 was checked against Appendix equations 36-37: the main i/n knot makes its final ReLU feature identically zero, whereas the appendix uses x_(i-1). Eleven primary-source foundations and competitors were checked on arXiv and official NeurIPS proceedings on 2026-08-23, covering kernel spectra, Fourier features, periodic/band-limited/wavelet/variable-periodic activations, realistic classification diagnostics, feature-learning dynamics, explicit reparameterization, and B-spline-constrained ReLU networks.
